fetched_contents.text: Antitakeover provisions, managerial entrenchment and firm innovation Highlights * • We explore the relation between antitakeover provisions and firm performance in innovation. * • We measure innovation by the number of patents and number of citations to patents. * • Managers who are protected from takeover market perform worse on innovation. * • Negative relation between antitakeover provisions and firm innovation holds only for low-tech firms. * • Results support agency based explanation of the relation between antitakeover provisions and performance in innovation. Abstract We explore the relation between antitakeover provisions (i.e. managerial entrenchment) and firm performance in innovation. Empirical results indicate that an increase in antitakeover provisions is negatively related to number of patents and number of citations to patents. Thus managers who are protected from takeover market perform worse on innovation. However, the negative relation between antitakeover provisions and firm innovation holds only for low-tech firms. For high-tech firms, this relation is not statistically significant. One possible explanation is that high-tech firms have to innovate continuously to survive in the long run. The competitive pressure to innovate or perish dissipates the negative effect of managerial entrenchment on firm innovation. Overall, our results support the agency based explanation of the relation between antitakeover provisions and firm performance in innovation. JEL classification O16 ; O31 ; O32 ; G31 ; G34 Keywords Patents ; Citations ; R&D ; Entrenchment ; Corporate governance Introduction Firm innovation plays a critical role in creating, sustaining and adding firm value. However, investment in innovative activities is a higher risk investment compared to investment in capital expenditures due to higher probability of failure (Bhagat and Welch, 1995, Holmstrom, 1989). Since R&D expenditures cannot be capitalized, investment in innovation depresses short term accounting earnings and reduces accounting based bonuses for managers. Moreover, investment in innovation is characterized by long gestation periods as cash flows could stretch beyond the tenures of managers (Dechow and Sloan, 1991, Gibbons and Murphy, 1992). Consequently, risk-averse managers may not have incentives to invest in innovation. However, firms that do not innovate lose market value and become desirable takeover targets. Thus the presence of an active external control market disciplines managers and forces them to invest in risky but value-maximizing projects. Managers do not like the takeover pressures and have incentives to favor antitakeover provisions that protect them from such pressures. Although antitakeover provisions have been studied in literature, there is no theoretical consensus on their effect on firm innovation. The agency cost based “managerial entrenchment hypothesis” argues that protecting managers from market for corporate control makes management more entrenched and further misaligns the interests of managers from those of shareholders (DeAngelo and Rice, 1983, Jensen and Meckling, 1976, Jensen and Ruback, 1983). The managerial entrenchment view thus predicts that antitakeover provisions increase entrenchment and negatively affect managerial incentives to innovate. On the other hand, the “managerial myopia hypothesis” asserts that the threat of a hostile takeover and the resulting career concerns about possible job loss make managers myopic and force them to make short-sighted investment decisions (Scherer, 1982, Stein, 1988). Stein (1988) argues that shareholders cannot value investments in innovation due to information asymmetry and drive down the market value of companies that make such investments, exposing these companies to takeover threats. Consequently, managers invest only in short term projects that the market can easily evaluate and avoid making investments in long term innovative projects. Protecting managers from takeover threats encourages them to take long term view and invest in innovation. Thus the managerial myopia view predicts a positive relation between antitakeover provisions and firm innovation. Given the absence of theoretical consensus, the relation between antitakeover provisions and firm innovation is an empirical question. This paper estimates the relation between antitakeover provisions and firm innovation. Following the current literature on antitakeover provisions, we call the presence of antitakeover provisions “managerial entrenchment”. Bebchuk, Cohen, and Ferrell (2009) construct an entrenchment index (E-index) from the corporate charter provisions of the Investor Responsibility Research Centre (IRRC). We use their index to measure managerial entrenchment. We use number of patents and number of citations to patents held by a firm to measure firm performance in innovation. Our results indicate that managerial entrenchment is negatively related to firm performance in innovation. An increase in entrenchment (i.e. increase in E-index) leads to poor performance on both measures of firm innovation. Prior research has shown that a subset of charter provisions that increases managerial entrenchment is associated with lower firm value (Bebchuk et al., 2009).1 Our results provide an explanation of the link between entrenchment and firm value – the same provisions that reduce firm value are also associated with lower performance in innovation. Thus, increased managerial entrenchment could lower firm value via its negative impact on firm innovation. We also examine if the relation between entrenchment and innovation is sensitive to industry characteristics. fetched_contents.text: DP RIETI Discussion Paper Series 10-E-022 Managerial Entrenchment and Anti-takeover Provisions in Japan HOSONO Kaoru Gakushuin University TAKIZAWA Miho Toyo University TSURU Kotaro RIETI The Research Institute of Economy, Trade and Industry http://www.rieti.go.jp/en/ RIETI Discussion Paper Series 10-E-022 Managerial Entrenchment and Anti-takeover Provisions in Japan Kaoru HOSONO* Miho TAKIZAWA** Kotaro TSURU*** First Draft: December 1, 2009 This Draft: March 17, 2010 Abstract In recent years, there has been an increase in the number of firms introducing anti-takeover provisions in Japan as well. In this paper, we analyze the characteristics of Japanese firms that introduced anti-takeover provisions during the four year period from fiscal 2005 to fiscal 2008, following the release of the official guidelines for anti-takeover provisions in 2005. Our main results are the following. First, firms' operating performance or stock market valuations were not related to the adoption of takeover defense measures. Second, firms' age and their ownership structure were correlated with the adoption of antitakeover provisions. Specifically, companies that were older, had lower proportions of shares held by their directors, or higher cross-shareholding ratios were more likely to adopt takeover defense measures, which suggests that the adoption of such measures is motivated by self-protection on the part of corporate managers and influenced by the conflicts of interest between managers and shareholders. In addition, as controlling shareholders had lower shares of stocks and institutional investors had higher shares of stocks, firms were more inclined to adopt takeover defense measures, suggesting that companies are likely to adopt such measures if their shares are liquid and easy to acquire. Key words: Antitakeover provisions, entrenchment, Japan. RIETI Discussion Papers Series aims at widely disseminating research results in the form of professional papers, thereby stimulating lively discussion. The views expressed in the papers are solely those of the author(s), and do not present those of the Research Institute of Economy, Trade and Industry. * Gakushuin University. Email kaoru.hosono@gakushuin.ac.jp ** Toyo University. *** Research Institute of Economy, Trade and Industr 1 Managerial Entrenchment and Antitakeover Provisions in Japan 1. Introduction Why do some firms adopt takeover defense measures and why do others not? Motivations for adopting antitakeover provisions have attracted many researchers interested in corporate governance as well as policymakers. If firms are more likely to adopt antitakeover provisions when their performance deteriorates or when managers behave themselves for their own interests, then antitakeover provisions prevent the takeover that would discipline managers and increase firm values without them (e.g., Manne, 1965). On the other hand, if firms tend to adopt antitakeover provisions when they are in the danger of the takeover that breaches trust among the stakeholders including managers and workers, then antitakeover provisions protect firms from the value-destroying takeover (e.g., Shleifer and Summers, 1988). We examine whether managers adopt antitakeover provisions for the purpose of managerial entrenchment, that is, to prevent themselves from losing their positions after takeovers. To this aim, Japanese experience servers as a quasi-natural experiment. In May 2005, the Japanese government released the guideline of antitakeover provisions, which endorsed Delaware takeover jurisprudence developed in the 1980s in the U.S. Since then, many firms adopted poison pills, though no firms had adopted antitakeover provisions before then. We consider the sudden emergence of antitakeover provisions in Japan as a good opportunity to study the relationship between ex ante firm characteristics and the decision whether or not to adopt antitakeover provisions. Without such an opportunity it would be difficult to distinguish the causal relationships between whether firm performance affects the decision of adopting antitakeover provisions or the adoption of antitakeover provisions affects firm performance. Distinguishing the causal relationship between the two is one of the most important contributions we make to the literature of antitakeover provisions. Using Japanese firm data over the period of 2005-2008, we investigate the relationship between ex-ante firm characteristics and the decision of adopting antitakeover provisions. Though some preceding studies apply event study methodologies to the U.S. firms to investigate how stock price responds to the announcement of adopting antitakeover provisions, event studies are difficult to apply to Japanese firms because Japanese firms often release many pieces of information besides antitakeover provisions at the same time. 2 Most of the preceding studies focused on firms in the U.S. (Malatesta and Walking, 1988; Mallette and Fower, 1992; Strong and Meyer, 1990; Davis, 1991; Davis and Stout, 1991; Sundaramurthy, 1996; Davis and Greve, 1997; Danielason and Karpoff, 1998). However, the recent wave of mergers and acquisitions including hostile takeovers is spreading over most industrial countries and emerging markets, though it was temporarily interrupted by the recent credit crisis. Abstract I study a protectionist anti-takeover law introduced in 2014 that covers a subset of all firms in the economy. The law decreased affected firms’ likelihood of becoming the target of a merger or acquisition and had a negative impact on shareholder value. There is no evidence that management of those firms subsequently altered firm policies in its interest. Investment, employment, wages, profitability, and capital structure remain unchanged. The share of annual CEO compensation consisting of equity instruments increased by 8.4 percentage points, suggesting that boards reacted to the loss in monitoring by the takeover market by increasing the pay-for-performance sensitivity. Introduction Over the last few years, governments worldwide have intervened in a significant number of cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&A), often citing national security concerns. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), the agency charged with evaluating the national security implications of foreign investments in the US, for example, conducted investigations into 66 transactions in 2015 (Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, 2017). Elected officials from France, Italy, and Germany have been advocating the introduction of a similar approval process in the European Union, and various European governments have recently given national agencies additional powers to intervene in inbound cross-border mergers and acquisitions (France in 2014 and Germany in 2017) or are currently contemplating doing so (e.g., the United Kingdom).1 As these protectionist interventions are likely to continue, it is important to ask if and to what extent they affect companies and their shareholders. Finance theory suggests that any action that reduces the threat of a takeover has the potential to entrench management at the expense of shareholders Manne (1965). I test whether protectionist anti-takeover legislation leads to managerial entrenchment based on the Alstom Decree, a protectionist law introduced in France in 2014. I use the Alstom Decree as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate the impact of protectionist anti-takeover legislation on firms’ investment and employment policies, operating performance, capital structure, cash distributions to shareholders, and executive compensation. Although there is a large literature studying the connection between managerial entrenchment and anti-takeover legislation, it is unclear whether its results should apply to today’s protectionist interventions.2 Protectionism decreases affected firms’ likelihood of receiving a takeover bid but does not necessarily affect management’s bargaining power if a bid is received. The anti-takeover laws studied by the literature on the other hand were explicitly designed to improve target management’s bargaining position in corporate transactions. In addition, most of the published results are based on data and events from the 1980s. But corporate governance standards worldwide have become significantly stricter over the last two decades in the wake of the collapse of, for example, Enron and WorldCom in the US and Parmalat in Europe, making it unclear whether takeovers as a governance mechanism should still have the same relevance today.3 The Alstom Decree designates the five industry sectors energy, water supply, transportation, electronic communications, and public health, which together account for around 30% of all publicly traded French firms, as strategic to the country’s interest and enables the secretary of commerce to veto M&A transactions targeting companies operating in them if the bidder originates from abroad. Since the introduction of the Alstom Decree until early 2018, over a hundred transactions have been the subject of an investigation. In addition, the law also has the potential to deter M&A transactions ex ante (also see Dinc and Erel, 2013), either because it increases the costs for the bidder through delays or less favorable deal terms or because the acquirer suspects the transaction might not find approval. I begin my investigation of the Alstom Decree by conducting a difference-in-differences analysis for firms’ probability of being acquired on a panel of both publicly listed and privately held French firms. I find that treated firms face a 0.8 percentage point lower annual probability of being acquired following the legislation, amounting to 40% of the unconditional probability, and that this effect is driven by a decrease in the probability of a cross-border acquisition. I further conduct an event study around the Alstom Decree’s announcement on May 14, 2014 to study its impact on shareholder value. The results indicate that a portfolio holding a long position in treated firms (i.e., firms subject to the Decree) and a short position of the same size in non-treated French firms would have generated statistically significant cumulative abnormal returns of between −0.59% and −0.98% over the event window. I then test whether the measurable decrease in the threat of a takeover affected corporate policies and monitoring at affected firms through additional difference-in-differences estimates. Branch report on the hypothesis’s theoretical assumptions

The managerial entrenchment hypothesis in the context of antitakeover provisions is fundamentally a theory about how corporate governance structures and takeover defenses shape managerial retention and firm performance. At its core, it claims that antitakeover provisions increase managerial entrenchment by reducing the threat of external takeovers, thereby making managers less responsive to market discipline and more likely to act in ways that protect their long-term control positions [N1-F1]. The literature summarized in the N1 evidence also frames the hypothesis as part of an agency-cost explanation, in which protecting managers from the market for corporate control makes their incentives misaligned with shareholders [N1-F1]. In other words, the hypothesis does not merely describe antitakeover provisions as a passive legal feature; it assumes that these provisions are strategically chosen or adopted because they serve managerial self-interest and reinforce managerial control [N1-F2].

A central assumption about managerial self-interest is that managers prefer to retain power and avoid the risk of being replaced in a takeover. The evidence from N1 shows that managers who are protected from takeover market pressure perform worse on innovation because they have less incentive to take risky but value-maximizing projects [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that managers are assumed to be risk-averse in the short run and less willing to invest in long-term innovation when they face a credible threat of takeovers [N1-F1]. The N2 evidence reinforces this by framing managerial entrenchment as a demand-side theory about managers’ reluctance to take on debt financing, suggesting a broader assumption that managers value discretion and control over financing choices [N2-R1]. Together, these sources imply that the hypothesis assumes managers are self-interested actors whose preferences are shaped by the presence or absence of takeovers as a disciplining mechanism [N1-F1][N2-R1].

The hypothesis also assumes that corporate governance plays a central role in shaping managerial behavior. The N1 evidence explicitly notes that the managerial entrenchment view predicts that antitakeover provisions increase entrenchment and negatively affect managerial incentives to innovate [N1-F1]. It further says that managers may have incentives to favor antitakeover provisions because they dislike takeover pressures [N1-F1]. This shows that corporate governance is not treated as a neutral institutional setting but as a mechanism through which managers can align their actions with retained control. The N2 evidence similarly implies that governance structure affects managerial behavior by linking entrenchment to capital structure and broader corporate governance components [N2-R1][N2-R5]. In addition, the N2 material includes a discussion of managerial entrenchment as a theory about the impact of governance on firm performance, which reinforces the assumption that governance arrangements are central to explaining how managers behave [N2-R2][N2-R5].

Overall, the theoretical assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis are threefold: first, that antitakeover provisions reduce the threat of takeovers and thereby increase managerial entrenchment; second, that managers are self-interested and have strong long-term control incentives, especially when takeovers are less likely; and third, that corporate governance structures are instrumental in shaping managerial behavior by altering the balance of power between managers and shareholders [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. These assumptions are consistent across the provided evidence, though they are not explicitly spelled out as a formal model in the excerpts; they are instead embedded in the theory of agency costs, governance effects, and the link between entrenchment and performance [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

Branch report on market and bidder-related assumptions

The market and bidder-related assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis are rooted in the idea that hostile takeovers are a meaningful threat that can discipline managers. The N1 evidence states that the agency cost-based managerial entrenchment hypothesis argues that protecting managers from the market for corporate control makes management more entrenched and further misaligns the interests of managers from those of shareholders [N1-F1]. This implies a key assumption: hostile takeovers are economically significant because they serve as a disciplining device that can constrain managers and improve firm value if the threat is credible [N1-F1]. The same source also says that firms that do not innovate lose market value and become desirable takeover targets, which underscores the assumption that the threat of takeovers can affect firm value through manager behavior [N1-F1].

A second assumption is that bidders are rational actors who respond to takeover opportunities in an economically efficient way. The N3 evidence provides direct support for this by discussing a protectionist anti-takeover law that decreased firms’ likelihood of becoming the target of a merger or acquisition and had a negative impact on shareholder value [N3-F3]. The excerpt also says that such legislation reduces the threat of a takeover, which is consistent with the assumption that bidders are sensitive to the presence of defenses and will adjust their bidding behavior accordingly [N3-F3]. The same evidence also notes that protectionist interventions can deter M&A transactions ex ante, either through increased costs for the bidder or through the acquirer’s suspicion that approval may be difficult [N3-F3]. This supports the assumption that bidders are rational and that takeover efficiency depends on the relative costs, risks, and expected payoffs of acquiring a target [N3-F3].

A third assumption is that antitakeover provisions alter bidder decision-making by making targets less attractive or harder to acquire. The N3 evidence explicitly says that protectionist anti-takeover legislation decreases the likelihood of receiving a takeover bid and that the law was used as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate its effects on firms’ policies and monitoring [N3-F3]. It also says that the law decreased the probability of cross-border acquisitions, which implies that bidder behavior is affected by the presence of defenses [N3-F3]. In addition, the broader literature summarized in N1 says that any action that reduces the threat of a takeover has the potential to entrench management at the expense of shareholders [N1-F2]. This reinforces the assumption that bidder rationality and takeover efficiency are affected by the defensive posture of the target, with stronger defenses making takeovers less likely and bidders more cautious or less willing to bid [N1-F2][N3-F3].

Taken together, the market and bidder-related assumptions are that hostile takeovers are a credible and economically significant threat, that bidders are rational and responsive to takeover opportunities, and that antitakeover provisions change bidder decision-making by reducing the attractiveness or feasibility of acquisitions [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-F2]. These assumptions underpin the hypothesis that managerial entrenchment occurs when takeovers are less threatening, which in turn changes how managers behave and how bidders act [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Branch report on informational and institutional assumptions

The informational and institutional assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis are critical because they explain why managers are assumed to benefit from antitakeover provisions and why outside investors are assumed to have less ability to monitor or discipline them. The N1 evidence states that the managerial myopia hypothesis asserts that the threat of a hostile takeover and the resulting career concerns make managers myopic and force them to make short-sighted investment decisions [N1-F1]. This assumption is directly related to information asymmetry: if managers know more than investors about the long-term value of projects, they may be able to pursue projects that are not immediately visible to outside investors [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that shareholders cannot value investments in innovation due to information asymmetry and drive down the market value of companies that make such investments [N1-F1]. This supports the assumption that information asymmetry between managers and outside investors is a key mechanism in the hypothesis [N1-F1].

A related assumption is that monitoring costs are important and that managerial information can have real value. The N4 evidence includes a study that says lower entrenchment leads to lower cash balances and higher marginal value of cash, while better monitoring leads to higher cash balances and lower marginal values of cash [N4-R1]. Although this is not directly about antitakeover provisions, it is consistent with the broader assumption that monitoring is costly and that managers’ information about the firm may affect how outside investors evaluate its value [N4-R1]. The N4 evidence also notes that Jensen’s free cash flow theory suggests managers prefer to retain rather than distribute excess cash absent positive net present value investment opportunities [N4-R4]. This implies that the value of managerial information lies in its ability to guide investment and cash management decisions, which are difficult for outside investors to monitor [N4-R4].

The credibility and enforceability of antitakeover provisions are also central to the hypothesis. The N1 evidence says that the managerial entrenchment view predicts that antitakeover provisions increase entrenchment and negatively affect managerial incentives to innovate [N1-F1]. It also says that managers who are protected from takeover market pressure perform worse on innovation [N1-F1]. This implies that the provisions are assumed to be credible and enforceable enough to actually alter managerial behavior, rather than merely being symbolic or ineffective [N1-F1]. The N3 evidence further supports this by showing that protectionist anti-takeover legislation decreased the likelihood of receiving a takeover bid and had a measurable effect on shareholder value, suggesting that the institutional arrangement is treated as credible enough to affect both target behavior and bidder behavior [N3-F3]. The same evidence also says that the law was used as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate its effects on firms’ policies and monitoring, reinforcing the assumption that the provisions are institutional arrangements with real enforceable consequences [N3-F3].

In summary, the informational and institutional assumptions are that managers have private information that outside investors cannot easily observe, that monitoring is costly and therefore valuable, and that antitakeover provisions are credible and enforceable enough to change managerial incentives and firm behavior [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4][N3-F3]. These assumptions are necessary for the hypothesis because they explain why managers would adopt or support antitakeover provisions and why outside investors would be less able to discipline them [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Branch report on empirical and methodological assumptions

The empirical and methodological assumptions underlying studies of antitakeover provisions are primarily about how researchers identify causal effects, how they select samples and handle data quality, and how they choose proxies and control variables. The N1 evidence shows that the literature on antitakeover provisions is concerned with distinguishing causal relationships from mere correlation, because it says that distinguishing the causal relationship between firm performance and the decision to adopt antitakeover provisions is one of the most important contributions to the literature [N1-F2]. This directly supports the assumption that empirical studies must be careful not to confuse correlation with causation when examining the relationship between provisions and outcomes [N1-F2].

Sample selection and data quality are also major concerns. The N1 evidence notes that the Japanese study examined firms introduced antitakeover provisions between fiscal 2005 and 2008 and used the sudden emergence of provisions as a quasi-natural experiment [N1-F2]. This implies that researchers assume that a sudden policy change or institutional shift can help identify causal effects, but also that they must be careful about selection bias and endogeneity [N1-F2]. The N5 evidence reinforces this by showing that one study evaluates the qualitative effect of corporate governance components, including a managerial entrenchment index, and that the purpose is to assess how governance relates to liquidity and risk management policies [N5-R1][N5-R4]. This suggests that empirical studies assume that governance-related proxies can be measured and that the data are sufficiently rich to support such analysis, but also that measurement error and data limitations are important methodological issues [N5-R1][N5-R4].

The choice of proxies and control variables is another key assumption. The N1 evidence says that the study uses an entrenchment index based on corporate charter provisions and measures innovation using patents and patent citations [N1-F1]. This indicates that researchers assume that such proxies are valid measures of managerial entrenchment and that innovation can be measured in a way that is sensitive to governance effects [N1-F1]. The N5 evidence also mentions studies that use managerial entrenchment indices, dividend policy analysis, and other governance components, which supports the assumption that researchers rely on proxies that are expected to capture governance-related behavior [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. The N5 material also includes a study on monitoring, managerial entrenchment, and liquidity/risk management policies, which implies that researchers assume that governance variables can be operationally defined and that control variables are needed to isolate the effects of entrenchment from other firm characteristics [N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the empirical and methodological assumptions are that causal effects must be identified carefully, that sample selection is important and that endogeneity can be addressed with quasi-experimental designs, that data quality and measurement validity matter, and that proxies and control variables must be chosen in a way that reflects the underlying theory [N1-F2][N1-F2][N5-R1][N5-R4]. These assumptions are necessary because they determine whether empirical findings can be interpreted as evidence for the managerial entrenchment hypothesis or as artifacts of correlation and model specification [N1-F2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

The bid-resistance and target-manager incentives branch of the managerial entrenchment hypothesis is centered on the idea that target managers may resist bids even when it is economically inefficient, because they have strong self-interest in retaining control. The N6 evidence explicitly states that under the managerial entrenchment hypothesis, target managers possess no incentives to negotiate for a bid revision, regardless of bid quality [N6-R1]. This is a central assumption: managers are assumed to value control and to resist any change in ownership structure, even if a higher-quality bid would otherwise be beneficial to shareholders [N6-R1]. The same evidence also says that the paper examines management’s motives for rejecting takeover bids and the associated shareholder wealth effects [N6-R2], which supports the broader assumption that managers are not purely profit-maximizing actors but are instead motivated by personal interests and control retention [N6-R2].

A key assumption about bid quality is that higher-quality bids are less likely to be rejected, while lower-quality bids are more likely to provoke resistance. The N6 evidence reports that the likelihood of higher follow-on offers decreases in bid quality and is greater when targets have classified boards and CEOs have significant personal wealth tied to the transaction [N6-R1]. This implies that the hypothesis assumes bid quality matters for bidder behavior and that managers may use resistance to pressure bidders into paying more or to signal that the firm is difficult to acquire [N6-R1]. The evidence also says that CEOs who fail to close high-quality offers experience a significant rate of forced turnover [N6-R1], which reinforces the assumption that managers have strong incentives to resist bids that could lead to their displacement [N6-R1].

The credibility of resistance and bidder response are also important assumptions. The N6 evidence finds a significant negative correlation between contested offers and bid quality, and that the likelihood of higher follow-on offers decreases in bid quality [N6-R1]. This supports the assumption that resistance can be credible enough to affect bidder behavior, because bidders may respond by increasing their offers or by reconsidering the transaction [N6-R1]. The broader literature summarized in N1 also says that the managerial entrenchment view predicts that antitakeover provisions increase entrenchment and misalign managerial incentives [N1-F1], which implies that resistance is credible when managers have the legal or institutional tools to enforce it [N1-F1]. The N3 evidence further supports this by showing that protectionist anti-takeover legislation decreased the likelihood of receiving a takeover bid and that such laws can deter M&A transactions ex ante [N3-F3]. Although this is not about bid resistance per se, it shows that bidder response depends on the institutional environment and that managers can use defensive provisions to make bids less attractive or more uncertain [N3-F3].

In summary, the bid-resistance and target-manager incentives assumptions are that managers have no incentive to negotiate for bid revisions, that bid quality matters for resistance and bidder response, and that resistance can be credible enough to influence bidder behavior and the likelihood of follow-on offers [N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3]. These assumptions are consistent with the broader managerial entrenchment hypothesis that managerial self-interest and control incentives drive resistance to takeovers [N1-F1][N6-R1].

## Integrated final answer: the fundamental assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis

The managerial entrenchment hypothesis regarding antitakeover provisions rests on a coherent set of assumptions that link corporate governance, managerial incentives, takeover threats, and firm behavior. At its core, the hypothesis assumes that antitakeover provisions reduce the threat of hostile takeovers and thereby increase managerial entrenchment, which in turn weakens market discipline and misaligns managerial incentives with shareholder interests [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This makes the hypothesis fundamentally a theory of corporate governance and agency conflict, not merely a descriptive account of takeover defense mechanisms [N1-F1][N2-R2].

### 1) Theoretical assumptions: managerial retention, self-interest, and governance

The hypothesis assumes that **antitakeover provisions are used by managers to retain control and protect their long-term positions**. The evidence shows that the managerial entrenchment view predicts that these provisions increase entrenchment and negatively affect managerial incentives to innovate [N1-F1]. It also says that managers who are protected from takeover market pressure perform worse on innovation because they have less incentive to take risky but value-maximizing projects [N1-F1]. This directly supports the assumption that managers are **self-interested actors** whose behavior is shaped by the perceived risk of being replaced or disciplined by the market [N1-F1][N2-R1].

A second theoretical assumption is that **managers have strong long-term control incentives**. The evidence frames managerial entrenchment as a demand-side theory about managers’ reluctance to take on debt financing, which implies that managers value discretion and control over financing choices [N2-R1]. More broadly, the hypothesis assumes that managers prefer to retain power and avoid the short-term risks associated with a hostile takeover or a change in ownership [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the idea that managerial self-interest is not only about personal wealth or compensation but also about preserving long-term control and influence [N2-R5][N1-F1].

A third assumption is that **corporate governance structures are central to shaping managerial behavior**. The evidence repeatedly treats governance as an institutional mechanism through which managers’ incentives are altered. The N1 evidence says that the managerial entrenchment view is part of an agency-cost explanation, and that the presence of antitakeover provisions changes the balance of power between managers and shareholders [N1-F1]. The N2 evidence similarly links managerial entrenchment to capital structure and to broader corporate governance components, showing that governance is not treated as a passive framework but as an active determinant of behavior [N2-R1][N2-R5]. In short, the hypothesis assumes that corporate governance is a key shaping force in managerial decision-making [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

### 2) Market and bidder-related assumptions

The hypothesis also depends on assumptions about the **threat of hostile takeovers and their economic significance**. The bid-resistance branch of the hypothesis assumes that **target managers have little incentive to negotiate for a bid revision**, even when the bid is high quality. The hypothesis relies on assumptions about **information asymmetry between managers and outside investors**. Finally, the hypothesis depends on empirical and methodological assumptions about how researchers identify causality, select samples, and construct proxies. The fundamental assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis are therefore:

The choice of proxies and control variables is another key assumption. Overall, the empirical assumptions are that researchers must identify causal effects carefully, that data and sample choices matter, and that proxies and controls must be chosen in a way consistent with the underlying theory [N1-F2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

## Conclusion

The fundamental assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis are therefore:

1. Antitakeover provisions reduce the threat of hostile takeovers and thereby increase managerial entrenchment [N1-F1][N1-F2].
2. Managers are self-interested and have strong long-term control incentives, especially when takeovers are less likely [N1-F1][N2-R1].
3. Corporate governance structures are central to shaping managerial behavior and altering the balance of power between managers and shareholders [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
4. Hostile takeovers are a credible and economically significant threat that disciplines managers and affects firm value [N1-F1][N3-F3].
5. Bidders are rational and responsive to takeover opportunities, and antitakeover provisions change bidder decision-making by making targets less attractive or harder to acquire [N1-F2][N3-F3].
6. Target managers often lack incentive to negotiate for bid revisions, and bid quality matters for resistance and bidder response [N6-R1][N6-R2].
7. Information asymmetry is important, monitoring costs matter, and managerial information can have real value [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].
8. Antitakeover provisions are assumed to be credible and enforceable enough to change managerial incentives and firm behavior [N1-F1][N3-F3].
9. Empirical studies must distinguish causal effects from correlation, carefully select samples and data, and choose proxies and control variables that reflect the theory [N1-F2][N5-R1][N5-R4].

These assumptions together make the managerial entrenchment hypothesis a theory of how corporate governance, managerial self-interest, and takeover defenses interact to shape firm behavior and outcomes [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F3][N6-R1][N4-R1][N5-R1].

## Integrated final answer: the fundamental assumptions underlying the managerial entrenchment hypothesis

The managerial entrenchment hypothesis regarding antitakeover provisions rests on a coherent set of assumptions that link corporate governance, managerial incentives, takeover threats, and firm behavior. At its core, the hypothesis assumes that antitakeover provisions reduce the threat of hostile takeovers and thereby increase managerial entrenchment, which in turn weakens market discipline and misaligns managerial incentives with shareholder interests [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This makes the hypothesis fundamentally a theory of corporate governance and agency conflict, not merely a descriptive account of takeover defense mechanisms [N1-F1][N2-R2].

### 1) Theoretical assumptions: managerial retention, self-interest, and governance

The hypothesis assumes that **antitakeover provisions are used by managers to retain control and protect their long-term positions**. The evidence shows that the managerial entrenchment view predicts that these provisions increase entrenchment and negatively affect managerial incentives to innovate [N1-F1]. It also says that managers who are protected from takeover market pressure perform worse on innovation because they have less incentive to take risky but value-maximizing projects [N1-F1]. This directly supports the assumption that managers are **self-interested actors** whose behavior is shaped by the perceived risk of being replaced or disciplined by the market [N1-F1][N2-R1].

A second theoretical assumption is that **managers have strong long-term control incentives**. The evidence frames managerial entrenchment as a demand-side theory about managers’ reluctance to take on debt financing, which implies that managers value discretion and control over financing choices [N2-R1].
